chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
title: Spring 1927 road trip, Cork O'Keefe and decline of the dance business
summary: O'Keefe booked a road trip finishing in Atlantic City while radio began to hurt dance business and tunes lasted longer.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Yes, they had soloists and they had a good ensemble. We used to judge a band a lot by its ensemble. If it had a good swinging and good moving ensemble, why, that was a plus. Well, then there comes along more toward spring and the band goes on the road for a month.
Now this is the spring of '28?
This is the spring of '27. Still '27 and Cork O'Keefe comes to manage the band and I think he booked the band on the road trip and he had a desk in the office and he and I roomed together.
Where did he work out of? Detroit.

Well, he had been, I think, in Philadelphia; but he came out there and I think he told me later that Goldkette wanted him to come out there and do a lot of booking for the band. Anyway, the band went on a road trip which was to finish off in the month of August in Atlantic City. Well, I guess the road trip in some places, you know, theaters and a couple of places, was quite good, but it got to be a little bit disastrous and if you check back at that particular time the business was beginning to get disastrous for dance bands.

I think radio had been making a few strides towards coming -- towards becoming more prominent and more of a business and the people were beginning to lose interest in dancing, going out to places to dance. Now, so they went through that, and in the meantime I was asked in Detroit if I wouldn't work while the band's on the road, because they were doing one-nighters mostly. You couldn't get to them, couldn't rehearse anything, couldn't get anything, didn't need anything.
Also, another item is that back in those days a

tune could be a hit for about two years. They didn't have the means of communication that they have today. You put a tune out and the next week, you don't know what's going to happen to it. But at least a tune has to be out now four to six weeks anyway and it's heard, and you know, you hear about it.
